clue.text: Drama when you take your Christmas decorations down?

definitions.meaning: A Shakespeare comedy, a play for the stage

definitions.text: when you take your Christmas decorations down?
definitions.meaning: by tradition decorations come down on the ... after Christmas, 5 or 6 January

explanation.surface: A wry question asking which play suits the evening the tinsel is packed away.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespeare comedy shares its title with the traditional evening, early in January, for clearing away festive trimmings.

clue.text: Doctor manic 'cos he's put his foot in it?

definitions.text: he's put his foot in it
definitions.note: a moccasin is a soft shoe, literally something a foot goes into

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A frantic man has blundered and said the wrong thing because of his mania.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person but is the anagram signal on MANICCOS. 'Put his foot in it' reads as an idiom for a gaffe; taken literally it points to footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A moccasin is a soft leather slipper-like shoe, so the wearer's foot literally goes inside one.

clue.text: Grumble head of branch has put up charge

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only the start of branch is used
in a down clue, put up means the word for charge is written bottom to top

parts.note: a fee is a charge for a service

explanation.surface: A complaint that the manager of a bank branch has increased fees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns FEE into EEF, which goes under B.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is informal slang for a complaint, as in having a beef with someone.

clue.text: Argues ecstasy is in short supply

parts.note: to spar is to argue or bicker, so argues gives spars
E is the common abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone claims that the drug ecstasy is hard to obtain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sparse is thinly spread or scanty, which is to say scarce.

clue.text: Extremely clever newspaper man? You owe him

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters, so only the outside of clever is taken

parts.note: an editor is the person in charge of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A sharp newspaper chief who, it turns out, has lent you money.
explanation.definitionFit: A creditor is a person to whom a debt is owed.

clue.text: Sleeps on way north, being cross

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading north means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: naps are short sleeps

explanation.surface: Someone dozing on a northbound journey wakes up in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like an adjective for angry; here it is the verb, as in crossing a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To span a gap, such as a river, is to stretch across it, as a bridge does.

clue.text: Complete dump, according to reports

indicators.note: reports are things heard, so this signals a word that sounds like another

parts.note: a hole is slang for a squalid, untidy place, a dump

explanation.surface: A judgement that a place is a total tip, based on hearsay.
explanation.definitionFit: Whole means entire or with nothing missing, the same as complete.

clue.text: No vegetarian would swallow such a lie!

definitions.text: No vegetarian would swallow such a lie!

parts.words: No vegetarian would swallow such a lie!
parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang a pie made of pork rhymes with lie, and a meat pie is something no vegetarian would eat

explanation.surface: An outraged retort that a claim is too unbelievable for anyone, vegetarian or not, to accept.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang uses 'porky pies' or 'pork pie' for lies; a pork pie is a British meat pastry. Both senses of 'swallow' apply: believe and eat.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang the meat pastry stands for a fib, while literally it is food a non-meat-eater refuses.

clue.text: Annoying expats I anger anew

indicators.note: anew means afresh or in a new way, so the letters are made over in a new order

explanation.surface: British expats provoke the locals all over again.
explanation.definitionFit: Exasperating describes something that irritates intensely, a stronger synonym for annoying.

clue.text: A match once for the Devil

definitions.meaning: an early friction match of the nineteenth century

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a contest long ago against Satan himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucifer was a trade name for early strike-anywhere matches and is also a traditional name for Satan.

clue.text: Some abandon Nairobi woman

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A woman who leaves Nairobi behind, or some people deserting the Kenyan capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna is an Italian word for a lady, used in English as a woman's title or simply a woman's name.

clue.text: Proof statement has been altered

indicators.note: altered means changed, so the letters of the word statement are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Evidence that a witness's statement has been tampered with.
explanation.definitionFit: A testament is something that serves as evidence, as in 'a testament to his skill'.

clue.text: Oddball diet not a cure

indicators.note: an oddball is something strange or eccentric, so the following letters are rearranged oddly

explanation.surface: A warning that an eccentric diet will not heal you.
explanation.definitionFit: An antidote is a remedy that counteracts a poison, so a cure.

clue.text: Airline quietly serving you bread roll

parts.note: BA is British Airways
p (piano) is the musical direction for playing quietly

explanation.surface: Cabin crew discreetly handing a passenger a sandwich roll.
explanation.walkthrough: A bap is a soft British bread roll.
explanation.definitionFit: A bap is a soft, round, flattish bun of the kind used for breakfast sandwiches in Britain.

clue.text: Knock down boyfriend at front of ship

parts.note: the bow is the forward end of a ship
a lover is a romantic partner, a boyfriend

explanation.surface: Someone flattens their boyfriend at the prow of a vessel, Titanic-style.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowl over is to knock someone to the ground, as by a rushing impact.

clue.text: Grandma's sister having change of heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, and here that letter is swapped for another

parts.note: a nun is a religious sister

explanation.surface: Granny's sister has suddenly changed her mind about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having change of heart' swaps the middle U of NUN for A.
explanation.definitionFit: Nan is an informal British word for a grandmother.

clue.text: Upper-class boozer holding raffle

indicators.note: one thing holding another contains it, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a toper is a heavy drinker
a draw is a lottery or raffle

explanation.surface: A posh drinker running a prize draw at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boozer' looks like a pub, which is the usual British sense; here it is the drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Top-drawer is an idiom for of the highest social class or quality.

clue.text: Personal assistant's attempt to make an eclair?

parts.note: PA is a personal assistant, and the possessive adds S
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: An office assistant trying their hand at baking a cream cake.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example: an eclair is one kind of pastry, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclair is a cream-filled cake of choux, an example of a pastry in the countable sense.

clue.text: £1000? That's good money for an Afrikaner

parts.note: the rand is the currency of South Africa, home of the Afrikaners

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a thousand pounds is a lot of cash to a South African.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand is slang for a thousand pounds or dollars.

clue.text: Unfortunately it's a girl, they say

indicators.note: what they say is spoken, so the answer sounds like the words given

parts.note: a lass is a girl, so a girl is a lass

explanation.surface: A disappointed parent announces the baby's sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of regret, used to mean sadly or regrettably.

clue.text: Occasionally smelly hooligan in successful show

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of smelly is taken

parts.note: a lout is a rough, aggressive young man

explanation.surface: A malodorous thug turns up in a hit production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' takes the odd letters S, E, L from smelly.
explanation.definitionFit: A sell-out is a performance for which every ticket has been bought, a sign of a hit.

clue.text: Want chess player to sacrifice bishop

indicators.note: sacrificing gives something up, so a letter is removed from the word

parts.note: Black is one of the two players in chess
B is the chess notation abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A chess player wishes to give up a bishop to gain an advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' looks like a verb, wish; it is the noun meaning shortage.
explanation.definitionFit: Want as a noun means a deficiency or absence, the same as lack.

clue.text: Raise a glass to Her Majesty's kitchen assistant?

parts.note: to toast someone is to raise a glass in their honour
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen

explanation.surface: A loyal toast to the Queen, then a nod to her kitchen helper.
explanation.definitionFit: A toaster is a small appliance that browns bread, a domestic helper in the kitchen.

clue.text: Wholesome French article in tin

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the article goes within the container word

parts.note: a can is a tin
le is the French masculine word for the

explanation.surface: A description of French food sold in tins as healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Clean in the moral sense means decent and inoffensive, as wholesome entertainment is.
